body: {"total":7,"records":[{"title":"Attendance at group pelvic floor muscle training for stress urinary incontinence: a systematic review of adherence and its predictors","authors":"Lindahl-Okafor B, Pritchard-Menon S, Vasquez-Aarts H","year":2021,"venue":"Journal of Pelvic Health Physiotherapy","doi":"10.5555/jphp.2021.0144","providerType":"review","abstract":"We reviewed 26 studies reporting attendance at group pelvic floor muscle training for women with stress urinary incontinence. In trials, women attended a median of 78 percent of sessions, but in the nine studies of routine services only 30 to 52 percent of referred women attended more than half of the sessions. Longer travel time, caring responsibilities and milder symptoms were the predictors most often reported, while group size and instructor were rarely studied. Most studies measured attendance from service records and predictors from referral data, and none linked patient-reported barriers to recorded attendance."},{"title":"Non-attendance at postnatal pelvic floor physiotherapy classes: a retrospective review of 1,204 referrals","authors":"Adebayo-Kristensen T, Moreau-Walsh E","year":2019,"venue":"Women's Health Physiotherapy Review","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We reviewed the records of 1,204 women referred to postnatal pelvic floor classes at one hospital over two years. Forty-one percent attended the first session and 23 percent attended four or more of six sessions. Non-attendance was more common in women aged under 25, in women living more than 20 kilometres from the hospital and in women whose records noted an interpreter need. Referral by a midwife rather than a doctor was not associated with attendance. Reasons for non-attendance were not recorded, and the review could not separate women who chose not to attend from those who could not."},{"title":"Why women do not come: a postal survey of barriers to pelvic floor classes among referred women","authors":"Harrington-Oduya P, Salgado-Lind M, Chen-Abara R","year":2022,"venue":"Physiotherapy Access and Equity","doi":"10.5555/pae.2022.0087","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We mailed a questionnaire to 860 women referred to group pelvic floor classes in one year; 327 replied (38 percent). Childcare was the most common barrier (46 percent), followed by embarrassment about discussing symptoms in a group (31 percent) and class times that clashed with work (29 percent). Non-attenders were less likely to reply than attenders (24 against 55 percent), so barriers among non-attenders are probably underestimated. Answers were not linked to attendance records, and the questionnaire was offered in English only."},{"title":"Evening and online pelvic floor classes and first-session attendance in a hospital physiotherapy service: a before-after comparison","authors":"Novak-Adeyemi J, Thornbury-Sato K","year":2023,"venue":"Journal of Pelvic Health Physiotherapy","doi":"10.5555/jphp.2023.0219","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"A hospital service added two evening classes and one live online class each week to its daytime group programme. Comparing 12 months before and after, first-session attendance rose from 44 to 63 percent and completion of four or more sessions from 26 to 37 percent. The rise was largest among women with children under five. Waiting time fell over the same period, which may explain part of the change, and the service did not collect reasons for non-attendance. Women attending online reported more technical problems in the first month, and women without home internet access used the evening classes instead."},{"title":"Pelvic floor class attendance across a regional physiotherapy network: service report","authors":"Regional Physiotherapy Network Quality Group","year":null,"venue":"Regional physiotherapy network internal report","providerType":"report","abstract":"This internal report summarises attendance at group pelvic floor classes in five hospital physiotherapy services. Completion of four or more sessions ranged from 19 to 44 percent between services. Services offering childcare-friendly times reported higher completion, but the report does not describe how attendance was counted, which months were included or how services were chosen. No statistical comparison was made, and the report carries no date, so it can only suggest where differences between services might lie. It was prepared for a network planning day and has not been reviewed outside the network."},{"title":"Language, interpreters and attendance at women's health physiotherapy: a cross-sectional study","authors":"Kaur-Ellison S, Mbatha-Frost D, Olsen-Achebe T","year":2017,"venue":"Physiotherapy Access and Equity","doi":"10.5555/pae.2017.0032","providerType":"cross-sectional study","abstract":"Using referral and attendance records for 2,310 women referred to women's health physiotherapy in two hospitals, we compared attendance by recorded language needs. Women who needed an interpreter were about half as likely to attend their first appointment (prevalence ratio 0.52, 95 percent CI 0.41 to 0.66) after adjustment for age and distance. Group classes had lower attendance than individual appointments for women needing an interpreter, and no class offered interpretation. Interpreter need was recorded inconsistently, so some women with limited English were probably classed as not needing one."},{"title":"Group versus individual pelvic floor muscle training: adherence in a randomised comparison","authors":"Brightwell-Nakamura A, Osei-Lundqvist F","year":2018,"venue":"Continence Care Research","doi":"10.5555/ccr.2018.0405","providerType":"Randomized Controlled Trial","abstract":"We randomly allocated 248 women with stress urinary incontinence to six weekly group classes or to individual sessions with the same exercises. Attendance at four or more sessions was similar (71 percent group, 74 percent individual), and improvement in leakage episodes did not differ at three months. Trial participants were volunteers who lived near the hospital, so attendance was much higher than in routine services. The group format cost less per woman treated. Women in the group arm said that meeting others with the same problem made it easier to keep going, although three withdrew because of the class times."}]}
